title: How China's DRAM Maker CXMT Caught Up With Micron Without EUV
gist: A short SemiWiki forum post pointing to a Liang-rong Chen piece arguing that China's CXMT has become the world's fourth-largest DRAM supplier by revenue, with DDR5 as its growth driver, and has narrowed the manufacturing cost gap with global leaders despite being barred from EUV lithography. The framing claim is that the next semiconductor battleground is memory rather than GPUs.

insights.claim: CXMT is now the world's fourth-largest DRAM supplier by revenue, with DDR5 rapidly becoming a major growth driver for the company.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: A credible fourth DRAM merchant supplier changes the oligopoly math that underpins Samsung/SK Hynix/Micron pricing power — watch DDR5 spot pricing and CXMT capacity announcements.

insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: If advanced DRAM cost parity is achievable without EUV, the export-control moat protecting incumbent memory margins is weaker than consensus assumes.

insights.claim: CXMT was founded roughly a decade ago, making its climb to top-four DRAM share unusually fast by semiconductor industry standards.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: The compressed timeline is the surprise variable — it compresses the window incumbents have to defend share before Chinese supply matters.

insights.claim: Export controls, EUV restrictions and industry skepticism were widely expected to cap China's memory ambitions, and CXMT's rise shows that expectation was wrong.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Suggests the policy premium priced into Western memory and litho names may be overstated; monitor whether restrictions get tightened in response.
insights.quote: For years, China's memory ambitions were overshadowed by export controls, EUV restrictions, and skepticism from the global semiconductor industry.

insights.claim: Industry attention focused on YMTC as China's memory champion while CXMT progressed with far less scrutiny.
